questions.q: Three children each have one fault. P has lost many teeth, Q cannot move her tongue properly, and R's food pipe walls do not contract and relax in waves. Each tries to eat a mouthful of chapati. State what goes wrong for each child.
questions.a: P: the chapati is not crushed and chewed into fine pieces, so mechanical digestion is poor. Q: the chewed food is not mixed with saliva and not pushed into the food pipe. R: the softened food is not pushed down the food pipe to the stomach.
s: P: no crushing into fine pieces
Q: no mixing with saliva and no pushing into the food pipe
R: no wave-like push down to the stomach

questions.q: True or False: A girl lying flat on her back can still swallow food, but only because gravity pulls the food down her food pipe. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The walls of the food pipe contract and relax in a wave-like motion that pushes the food down to the stomach; this push, not gravity alone, moves the food, and it works throughout the alimentary canal.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: wave-like contraction and relaxation of the walls pushes the food

questions.q: Tube A has unchewed boiled rice in water. Tube B has boiled rice that was chewed for a minute, in the same amount of water. Tube C has boiled rice that was only crushed to a paste with a spoon, with no saliva, in the same amount of water. Equal drops of iodine solution are added to all three. Which result is expected?
questions.a: Tubes A and C turn deep blue-black; tube B stays faint or colourless
o: Tubes A and C turn deep blue-black; tube B stays faint or colourless
Tubes A and B turn deep blue-black, while tube C stays faint because it was broken into small pieces
Tubes A, B and C all turn equally deep blue-black, because iodine only detects that rice is present
Tube A turns deep blue-black, while tubes B and C stay faint because both were broken up

questions.q: Dinesh finishes a plate of rice in 5 minutes, chewing each mouthful only a few times. His sister Pooja takes 20 minutes and chews each mouthful until the rice begins to taste sweet. Compare what each child sends down the food pipe and justify which child leaves the rest of the alimentary canal an easier job. Use points about the mouth stage only, and also say what even Pooja's chewing cannot finish.
questions.a: Pooja's food is crushed into fine pieces by chewing (mechanical digestion), while Dinesh's is in larger lumps. Her longer chewing gives saliva more time to break starch into sugar, which is why her rice tastes sweet. Her food is mixed with saliva by the tongue, soft and moist, and easy to swallow. So she sends partly digested, softened food on, and her later parts have an easier job. Even so, the food is only partially digested in the mouth; the rest of the digestion must still happen along the canal.
s: Fine pieces (mechanical digestion) for Pooja versus lumps for Dinesh
Longer time lets saliva change more starch into sugar
Moistened, soft food mixed by the tongue is easy to swallow
Judgement: Pooja leaves the canal an easier job
Digestion in the mouth is only partial, the rest happens later

questions.q:
After a fever, Sushma's mouth is very dry. She finds a dry chapati hard to swallow and not as sweet as usual after a minute of chewing.
(a) Which fluid of the mouth is she short of?
(b) Explain each of her two difficulties using the two jobs of this fluid.
questions.a: (a) Saliva. (b) Saliva moistens the food and makes it soft and easy to swallow, so with too little of it the chapati stays dry and hard to swallow. Saliva also contains a digestive juice that breaks starch into sugar, so with too little of it less starch becomes sugar and the chapati is not as sweet.
s: Part (a): saliva
Part (b): moistening for swallowing and starch to sugar for sweetness

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the mouth and the movement of food.
Statement 1: The crushing and chewing of food into fine pieces by the teeth is called mechanical digestion.
Statement 2: The wave-like movement of the walls that pushes food forward is found only in the food pipe.
Statement 3: Saliva is released only after food has entered the mouth.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 only
o: 1 only
2 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): In Activity 9.1 the chewed boiled rice in tube B shows a much lighter blue-black colour with iodine than the unchewed rice in tube A.
Reason (R): Chewing crushes the rice into fine pieces, and crushing removes the starch from it.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
At a school health camp, 40 children are asked about oral hygiene. Group X has 16 children who only brush their teeth twice a day; 10 of them have bad smell in the mouth. Group Y has 24 children who brush twice, clean the tongue twice and rinse the mouth with water after each meal; 6 of them have bad smell.
(a) Which two habits does group Y follow in addition to brushing, and what two problems does the book say the advice prevents?
(b) Work out the percentage with bad smell in each group.
(c) Can these figures show which of the two extra habits made the difference? Explain.
(d) The school can add only one 5-minute habit after lunch for all children. Decide between rinsing with water and a second brushing, and justify your decision.
questions.a: (a) Cleaning the tongue and rinsing the mouth with water after each meal; they prevent tooth decay and bad smell. (b) X: 10 of 16 = 62.5%. Y: 6 of 24 = 25%. (c) No. Group Y added both habits together, so the figures cannot say which one helped; they only show the fuller routine goes with less bad smell. (d) Rinsing with water, because the book advises rinsing after each meal, while brushing and tongue cleaning are advised twice a day; the other habits must still continue.
s: Part (a): tongue cleaning and rinsing; tooth decay and bad smell
Part (b): 62.5% and 25%
Part (c): both habits added together, so cannot separate
Part (d): rinse after the meal, reason from the book's advice

questions.q:
Kavya's class repeats the rice and iodine activity. Four groups chew boiled rice for different times before adding the same amount of iodine: group A does not chew, B chews for 15 s, C for 30 s and D for 60 s. The colours are deep blue-black (A), medium (B), light (C) and very faint (D). Each child eats about 25 mouthfuls at lunch, and the lunch break is 20 minutes. Assume chewing is the only time used.
(a) What does the colour of group A tell you about the rice, and why was A included?
(b) What trend do the colours show, and what does it say about saliva?
(c) How long would 25 mouthfuls take if each is chewed for 30 s, and for 60 s? Which fit the break?
(d) The class must advise Class 5 on how long to chew each mouthful. Decide and say what the advice gives up.
questions.a: (a) Unchewed rice gives deep blue-black, so the rice contains starch; A is the comparison that shows what chewing changed. (b) Longer chewing gives a lighter colour, so saliva breaks more starch into sugar as time passes. (c) 25 x 30 s = 750 s = 12.5 minutes, which fits; 25 x 60 s = 1500 s = 25 minutes, which does not fit the 20-minute break. (d) Advise about 30 s per mouthful: it is the lightest colour that fits the break; it gives up the very faint colour of 60 s, so a little more starch is left for later parts of the canal.
s: Part (a): starch present; A is the unchewed comparison
Part (b): longer chewing, lighter colour, saliva breaks down starch
Part (c): 12.5 min fits, 25 min does not
Part (d): 30 s, with what it gives up

questions.q: In Activity 9.1 a student finds that her chewed rice in tube B turns almost as deep blue-black as the unchewed rice in tube A. Write one situation that could explain this, say what the colour tells you about the starch in tube B, and say what the book suggests doing next.
questions.a: Situation: she chewed the rice for only a few seconds, so saliva had very little time to act. The deep colour shows that most of the starch in tube B is still present. The book suggests repeating the activity with a longer chewing time and comparing the colour.
s: Situation: chewing time too short for saliva to act
Deep colour means most starch is still present
Repeat with longer chewing and compare

questions.q: Nandini mashes a spoonful of boiled rice into a smooth paste with a spoon and does not put any of it in her mouth. Which statement about the paste is correct?
questions.a: It is broken into fine pieces, but its starch is still unchanged by mashing
o: It is broken into fine pieces, but its starch is still unchanged by mashing
Its starch has turned into sugar, so it would now taste sweet
It is fully digested, because fine pieces are a simpler form of food
It would show no blue-black colour with iodine, because mashing removes starch

questions.q: Aman says: 'Chewed rice in tube B gave almost no blue-black colour with iodine, so there was never any starch in the rice.' Do you agree? Give reasons.
questions.a: No. Tube A had the same rice unchewed and turned blue-black with iodine, which shows the rice contains starch. In tube B saliva had broken the starch down into simple sugars, which iodine does not turn blue-black.
s: Verdict: disagrees
Tube A with unchewed rice shows starch is present
In B saliva changed starch to sugar

questions.q:
Classify each as mechanical digestion or the action of the digestive juice in saliva, and give the sign that tells you which it is.
(i) A bite of roti is reduced to tiny bits by the molars.
(ii) A bite of roti begins to taste sweet after 40 s of chewing.
questions.a: (i) Mechanical digestion: the food is only crushed into smaller pieces, with nothing new formed. (ii) The digestive juice in saliva: the sweet taste shows starch has been changed into sugar.
s: (i) mechanical, only broken into pieces
(ii) saliva's juice, sweet taste shows sugar from starch

questions.q: After an injury to his tongue, Rahul finds that chewed rice stays scattered inside his mouth and he cannot push it towards his throat. Which two jobs of the tongue is he missing?
questions.a: Mixing food with saliva and pushing it into the food pipe
o: Mixing food with saliva and pushing it into the food pipe
Producing the saliva and changing starch into simple sugar
Crushing the food into fine pieces and moistening it
Squeezing food down the food pipe in waves and churning it

questions.q:
Match each situation in Column I with the part that explains it in Column II.
Column I: 1. A bite of roti becomes sweet only after a minute of chewing  2. A mouthful is broken into fine pieces  3. Chewed, softened food is moved from the mouth into a long tube  4. Food is pushed down to the stomach in waves
Column II: A. tongue  B. walls of the food pipe  C. teeth  D. digestive juice in saliva

Kavya wants to find out whether chewing for longer leaves less starch in rice. Plan an investigation: say what you will change, what you will keep the same, what you will observe, and what result would support the idea.
questions.a: Change: the time of chewing, for example 15 s, 30 s and 60 s. Keep same: amount of boiled rice, amount of water and number of drops of iodine. Observe: colour after adding iodine. Supporting result: the longer the chewing, the lighter the blue-black colour, because saliva has broken more starch into sugar.
s: Variable changed: chewing time
Two things kept the same
What is observed: iodine colour
Result that supports the idea
Reason from the action of saliva on starch

questions.q:
(a) In tube B of Activity 9.1 a very light blue-black colour still appears after the rice was chewed for 30 s. What does this tell you about the starch?
(b) Use your answer to explain why the book calls the digestion of food in the mouth 'partial'.
questions.a: (a) A very small amount of starch is still present; most of it has been broken down into sugars. (b) Some of the starch is changed in the mouth but not all, so the food leaves the mouth only partially digested and the rest of its digestion happens further along the alimentary canal.
s: Part (a): a very small amount of starch remains
Part (b): partial digestion, rest happens later in the canal

questions.q: Mina chews boiled rice for 30 s, puts it in water and adds iodine, but still sees a medium blue-black colour. Which next step does the book suggest to explore this?
questions.a: Repeat it with a longer chewing time and compare the colours again
o: Repeat it with a longer chewing time and compare the colours again
Add extra drops of iodine until the blue-black colour fades away
Warm the rice and water mixture slightly before adding the iodine
Use chapati instead of rice and swallow it without any chewing

questions.q: Ravi crushes a dry roti to a fine powder with a stone pestle, adding no saliva. The powder still turns deep blue-black with iodine. The only kind of digestion his crushing has carried out is ___ digestion.
questions.a: mechanical

questions.q:
Raju brushes his teeth twice a day. He rinses his mouth with water after lunch only, although he eats three meals a day, and he never cleans his tongue.
(a) Which parts of the book's oral hygiene advice does he not follow?
(b) Which two problems is that advice meant to prevent?
questions.a: (a) He does not clean his tongue twice a day, and he does not rinse after his other two meals. (b) Tooth decay and bad smell in the mouth.
s: Part (a): tongue cleaning and rinsing after every meal
Part (b): tooth decay and bad smell

questions.q: A student pours dilute acid into a beaker and then adds a mildly basic liquid until the mixture is neutral. Which pair of secretions does the same job on the acid that reaches the small intestine from the stomach?
questions.a: Bile from the liver and pancreatic juice from the pancreas
o: Bile from the liver and pancreatic juice from the pancreas
Saliva from the mouth and bile from the liver
Mucus of the stomach and pancreatic juice from the pancreas
Juice of the small intestine wall and the juice of the stomach

questions.q:
Ananya, 13, has celiac disease: gluten harms the inner lining of her small intestine. Today the canteen lists wheat sandwich Rs 25, barley soup Rs 20, bajra roti Rs 35, rye toast Rs 20, jowar upma Rs 30 and ragi dosa Rs 45. She has only Rs 50.
(a) Which three items contain gluten, according to your book?
(b) Which job of the small intestine is harmed in Ananya, and why does she feel weak even after a large meal?
(c) Can she buy two gluten-free items with Rs 50? Show it with the cheapest pair.
(d) Her friend says: 'Take barley soup and rye toast for Rs 40 and eat more.' Decide between that and one gluten-free item, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Wheat sandwich, barley soup and rye toast, because gluten is in wheat, barley and rye. (b) Absorption of nutrients: with a damaged lining, digested nutrients cannot pass properly into the blood, so the body does not get the energy and materials even from a large meal. (c) No. The cheapest safe pair is jowar upma Rs 30 + bajra roti Rs 35 = Rs 65, which is more than Rs 50, so she can buy only one safe item. (d) She should buy one gluten-free item such as the jowar upma at Rs 30: the cheaper gluten items would damage the lining further, and a larger meal does not help when the damaged lining cannot absorb nutrients; she gives up quantity, not safety.
s: Part (a): wheat, barley and rye items
Part (b): absorption lost, nutrients do not enter the blood
Part (c): cheapest safe pair Rs 65 exceeds Rs 50
Part (d): one safe item, with reason from the lining damage

questions.q: Rohan says: 'All the digestion of proteins, carbohydrates and fats is finished in the stomach.' Is he right? Support your answer with the work of the stomach and of the small intestine.
questions.a: No. The stomach's juice breaks down only proteins. Pancreatic juice acts on carbohydrates, proteins and fats, bile helps fats, and the intestine's own juice further breaks fats, proteins and partly digested carbohydrates. Digestion therefore continues in the small intestine.
s: Verdict: no
Stomach juice acts on proteins
Small intestine and its secretions complete digestion

questions.q: A classroom chart uses 1 cm of string for every 20 cm of real length. The string for the longest part of the alimentary canal, which is the part where digested food is absorbed, must be ___ cm long.
A mouthful of dal and rice reaches the stomach. Which description of what happens there is correct?
questions.a: The walls churn it, the juice acts on the dal's protein, mucus protects the lining, and a semi-liquid mass forms
o: The walls churn it, the juice acts on the dal's protein, mucus protects the lining, and a semi-liquid mass forms
The walls churn it, the juice changes the rice starch into sugar, and acid and mucus form a semi-liquid mass
The food is absorbed through the stomach wall into the blood, and only the rice moves on to the small intestine
The food stays unchanged in the stomach until it reaches the small intestine, where the acid begins to act

questions.q:
Two models of the inner lining of the small intestine have the same length and width. Model 1 is a smooth flat sheet. Model 2 is covered with thousands of tiny finger-like projections.
(a) Which model has the larger surface area?
(b) Which model better shows how the lining takes digested nutrients into the blood, and why?
questions.a: (a) Model 2. (b) Model 2, because the projections increase the surface area, so more of the digested food touches the lining and passes into the blood in the walls of the small intestine.
s: Part (a): the model with projections
Part (b): larger surface area gives efficient absorption into blood

questions.q: A meal of rice (starch), dal (protein) and ghee (fat) is eaten. For each of the three food components, trace the secretions that act on it from the mouth up to the small intestine, and say where the digested product finally goes. Then say which two secretions are shared by all three components after the stomach.
questions.a: Starch: saliva begins changing it to sugar in the mouth; pancreatic juice and the wall of the small intestine continue (partially digested carbohydrates). Protein: stomach juice (with acid) breaks it down; pancreatic juice and the intestinal wall juice continue. Fat: bile breaks it into tiny droplets; pancreatic juice and the intestinal wall juice break it down further. The digested products pass into the blood in the walls of the small intestine through its finger-like projections (absorption). Pancreatic juice and the juice of the intestinal wall act on all three components.
s: Starch path: saliva, pancreatic juice, intestinal wall juice
Protein path: stomach juice, pancreatic juice, intestinal wall juice
Fat path: bile droplets, pancreatic juice, intestinal wall juice
Absorption into the blood in the small intestine
Names pancreatic juice and intestinal wall juice as shared

questions.q: A drug destroys the mucus part of the stomach's secretion but leaves the acid and the digestive juice working. Predict what will happen to the stomach lining, and name the part of the secretion whose job is now missing.
questions.a: The acid will damage the stomach lining. The mucus is the part of the secretion that protects the lining from the acid, so its job is missing.
s: Prediction: acid damages the lining
Mucus is the protecting part

questions.q:
Match each effect in Column I with the source of the secretion responsible in Column II.
Column I: 1. Ghee fat is broken into tiny droplets and acid from the stomach is neutralised  2. A basic juice acts on carbohydrates, proteins and fats  3. Dal protein starts breaking down and many harmful bacteria are killed  4. Fats, proteins and partly digested carbohydrates are broken down further
Column II: A. liver  B. pancreas  C. lining of the stomach  D. wall of the small intestine

A student claims: 'The liver and the pancreas both neutralise the acid from the stomach, so the small intestine can do without one of them.' Test the claim. For the neutralising job, for the other jobs of each secretion, and for the secretion of the intestinal wall, say what is and is not covered, and give a verdict.
questions.a: Partly right. For neutralising acid, both bile and pancreatic juice are basic, so each can do it. But bile has a second job, breaking fats into tiny droplets, which pancreatic juice is not said to do. Pancreatic juice also breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats, which bile does not, and the wall of the small intestine only acts on fats, proteins and partially digested carbohydrates. So the neutralising job is shared, but the other jobs are not, and neither organ can be left out.
s: Both secretions are basic and neutralise acid
Bile's other job: tiny fat droplets
Pancreatic juice's other job: all three food components
Intestinal wall juice does not cover those jobs
Verdict: partly right

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bile from the liver helps neutralise the acid in food arriving from the stomach.
Reason (R): Bile is mildly basic in nature.
questions.a: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Dr Rao plans an operation after which food will go straight from the food pipe into the small intestine, leaving out the stomach. Predict three things that would no longer happen to a mouthful of dal and rice, and name one thing that would still happen in the small intestine.
questions.a: The walls of the stomach would no longer churn the food into a semi-liquid mass; the stomach juice would no longer start breaking down the dal's protein; the acid would no longer kill many harmful bacteria. In the small intestine the secretions would still act and the digested nutrients would still be absorbed into the blood.
s: No churning into semi-liquid mass
No stomach juice on protein and no acid killing bacteria
Small intestine still digests and absorbs

questions.q:
(a) Bile breaks the ghee fat of a meal into tiny droplets. Is this a step of digestion or of absorption?
(b) Glucose from rice then passes from the small intestine into the blood. Name this process and the feature of the lining that helps it.
questions.a: (a) A step of digestion, since a complex component is being broken down to make its digestion easier. (b) Absorption, helped by the thousands of finger-like projections on the inner lining that increase its surface area.
s: Part (a): digestion, breaking down food
Part (b): absorption with finger-like projections

questions.q:
Dr Mehta tests three patients after a meal of dal, rice and ghee. P makes very little stomach acid and juice. Q's liver makes very little bile. R's pancreas does not secrete pancreatic juice. She records the percentage of each food component broken down by the end of the small intestine, but the rows are not labelled:
Row X: starch 60, protein 50, fat 45.
Row Y: starch 90, protein 55, fat 85.
Row Z: starch 88, protein 85, fat 50.
(a) Match X, Y and Z to P, Q and R, giving your reason for each.
(b) Work out the average of the three percentages for each row. Which patient is worst off?
(c) Why does one patient's failure lower all three components while the others lower only one?
(d) At a festival Q can have either a ghee-rich meal or a dal-rich meal. Decide using the figures, and say why Q's fat digestion is not zero.
questions.a: (a) P = Y: only protein is low, as the stomach juice acts on proteins. Q = Z: only fat is low, as bile breaks fats into droplets. R = X: all three are low. (b) X: (60+50+45)/3 = 51.7. Y: (90+55+85)/3 = 76.7. Z: (88+85+50)/3 = 74.3. R is worst off. (c) Pancreatic juice acts on carbohydrates, proteins and fats, while the stomach juice acts on proteins and bile on fats. (d) The dal-rich meal, since Q breaks down 85% of protein but only 50% of fat; Q's fat digestion is not zero because pancreatic juice and the juice of the intestinal wall still act on fats.
s: Part (a): Y=P, Z=Q, X=R with reasons
Part (b): 51.7, 76.7, 74.3; R lowest
Part (c): pancreatic juice acts on all three components
Part (d): dal-rich meal, other juices still act on fat

questions.q: After an operation a man's liver can no longer secrete bile. Which pair of changes would you expect in the food entering his small intestine?
questions.a: Fat is not broken into droplets and acid is less neutralised
o: Fat is not broken into droplets and acid is less neutralised
Protein is not broken down and the acid is more strongly neutralised
Starch is not changed to sugar and fat is broken into tiny droplets
Nutrients cannot be absorbed and the acid is fully neutralised

questions.q:
(a) Give two jobs of the acid in the stomach.
(b) Using them, explain why a person who takes a medicine that greatly lowers the acid in the stomach may fall ill from harmful bacteria in food more easily.
questions.a: (a) It helps break down proteins and it kills many harmful bacteria. (b) With less acid, fewer of the harmful bacteria that enter with the food are killed, so more of them survive and can make the person ill.
s: Part (a): helps break down proteins, kills harmful bacteria
Part (b): fewer bacteria killed with less acid

questions.q: Two patients ate the same meal and both feel weak. In M the food is broken down properly but its nutrients fail to reach the blood. In N the nutrients are absorbed normally but the fat of the meal is not broken into tiny droplets. Which pair of causes is most likely?
questions.a: M: damaged finger-like projections in the small intestine; N: too little bile from the liver
o: M: damaged finger-like projections in the small intestine; N: too little bile from the liver
M: too little bile from the liver; N: damaged finger-like projections in the small intestine
M: too little mucus in the stomach; N: damage to the large intestine
M: too little saliva in the mouth; N: weak waves in the food pipe

questions.q: A friend says: 'If a person's liver makes no bile, none of the fat in his meal can be digested at all.' Show that this cannot be right, and say what is lost.
questions.a: The pancreatic juice of the pancreas still breaks down fats, and the juice of the wall of the small intestine further breaks down fats, so some fat digestion continues. What is lost is the breaking of fats into tiny droplets, which makes their digestion easier, and the help in neutralising acid.
s: Pancreatic juice still acts on fats
Intestinal wall juice still acts on fats
What is lost: tiny droplets and part of the neutralising

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the small intestine.
Statement 1: Pancreatic juice is basic and helps neutralise acids, and it also breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
Statement 2: The juice from the wall of the small intestine further breaks down fats, proteins and partially digested carbohydrates.
Statement 3: Digested nutrients pass into the blood through the walls of the stomach, which is where food becomes a semi-liquid mass.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only
o: 1 and 2 only
1 and 3 only
2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: Write a short case of a person whose digestion in the small intestine is normal but who still loses weight and feels weak. Name the part of the lining with the problem and say what fails to happen to the digested food.
questions.a: Case: a girl eats full meals and her digestive juices act normally, but the thousands of finger-like projections on the inner lining of her small intestine are damaged. The digested nutrients cannot pass efficiently into the blood in its walls, so absorption fails and she loses weight and feels weak.
s: Situation with the finger-like projections of the lining damaged
Digested nutrients fail to pass into the blood

questions.q: True or False: The large intestine gets its name because it is longer than the small intestine. Give the verdict and the reason.
questions.a: False. The large intestine is about 1.5 metres long, shorter than the almost 6 metre small intestine; it is called large because it is wider.
s: Verdict: false
Reason: shorter but wider than the small intestine

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bacteria living in the large intestine make the waste semi-solid by absorbing water from it.
Reason (R): The large intestine absorbs water and some salts from the undigested food.
questions.a: A is false but R is true.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: Seema says: 'Curd and buttermilk are good for digestion, so a child who has them every day does not need to eat fruits, vegetables or whole grains.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. Fermented foods such as curd and buttermilk are good for a healthy digestive system. But the claim that fibre-rich foods are not needed is wrong: fruits, vegetables and whole grains help the large intestine function properly by making the stool easier to pass, and the bacteria of the large intestine break down undigested food, especially fibre.
s: Verdict: partly right
Fermented foods are good for digestion
Fibre-rich foods are still needed to ease stool and for the bacteria's work

questions.q:
In a hostel of 40 children, 12 complained of hard stool when breakfast had little fibre. After a month of whole-grain rotis, fruit and vegetables, only 3 still complained; they eat the same meals but leave most of the vegetables on the plate. The warden can spend on one step: a fruit for all 40 children at Rs 8 each per day, or an extra serving of vegetables for the 3 children at Rs 3 each per day.
(a) Work out the percentage of children with hard stool before and after, and how many were relieved.
(b) In which part of the alimentary canal is the problem, and which food component of the new breakfast helped?
(c) How do the bacteria of that part work on this food component?
(d) Choose a step, give the daily cost of each, and justify.
questions.a: (a) Before: 12 of 40 = 30%. After: 3 of 40 = 7.5%. So 9 children were relieved. (b) The large intestine; the fibre of whole grains, fruits and vegetables helps it function by making the stool easier to pass. (c) The bacteria break down undigested food, especially fibre, and produce essential nutrients. (d) Extra vegetables for the 3 children: Rs 3 x 3 = Rs 9 a day, against Rs 8 x 40 = Rs 320 for the fruit. The 3 still have the problem because they leave the vegetables, so more fibre for them targets it; the whole-grain breakfast must continue for everyone.
s: Part (a): 30%, 7.5%, 9 children
Part (b): large intestine, fibre
Part (c): bacteria break down undigested food, especially fibre
Part (d): Rs 9 versus Rs 320, targeted step with reason

questions.q: Gaurav's day: a jam sandwich on bread with almost no fibre for breakfast, rice and dal for lunch, fried chips as a snack, and a dinner that he finishes in five minutes with a third helping. He has no fruit, curd or whole grain. Suggest three changes, one for the stool, one for the bacteria of the digestive system and one for mealtime habit, and say how each helps.
questions.a: Add fruits, vegetables or whole grains: fibre makes the stool easier to pass. Add a fermented food such as curd or buttermilk: fermented foods are good for the digestive system and its helpful bacteria. Eat mindfully and avoid overeating (no third helping): the book lists mindful eating and avoiding overeating as key for digestive health.
s: Fibre-rich food and how it eases stool
Fermented food and its benefit
Mindful eating or no overeating

questions.q: In a stretched-out model of the alimentary canal a student draws the small intestine as a string 60 cm long. To the same scale, how long should the string for the large intestine be?
questions.a: 15 cm
o: 15 cm
60 cm
240 cm
30 cm

questions.q:
Raj eats curd, buttermilk and pickle daily, but no fruit, vegetable or whole grain.
(a) Which of the two kinds of food that the book recommends for a healthy digestive system is he missing?
(b) Which part of his alimentary canal will notice this, and how?
questions.a: (a) Fibre-rich foods such as fruits, vegetables and whole grains. (b) The large intestine, which functions less well without fibre, so his stool may be harder to pass.
s: Part (a): fibre-rich foods
Part (b): large intestine, stool harder to pass

questions.q:
Using the lengths your book gives for the two intestines:
(a) How many times as long as the large intestine is the small intestine?
(b) A friend says the larger length must be the 'large' one. Reply to him with the book's reason for the names.
questions.a: (a) Small intestine almost 6 m, large intestine about 1.5 m, so 6 / 1.5 = 4 times. (b) The large intestine is shorter but wider than the small intestine, and that width is why it is called large.
s: Part (a): 6 / 1.5 = 4 times
Part (b): large because wider, though shorter

questions.q: A sample of undigested material taken from the start of a person's large intestine is watery, but a sample of the waste in the rectum of the same person is semi-solid. Which job of the large intestine explains the change?
questions.a: It takes water and some salts out of the undigested food as it passes
o: It takes water and some salts out of the undigested food as it passes
It breaks the fats of the food into tiny droplets in the liquid
It churns the whole food into a semi-liquid mass in the stomach
It passes digested nutrients on into the blood through its walls

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the end of the alimentary canal.
Statement 1: Stool is stored in the upper part of the large intestine until the body is ready to get rid of it.
Statement 2: Egestion is the expelling of the stool through the anus.
Statement 3: The large intestine absorbs water and some salts, which makes the waste semi-solid.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only
o: 2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
1 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q: A hostel plans lunch for 30 children. Menu 1: plain rice, fried chips and sweet jalebi. Menu 2: whole-wheat roti, mixed vegetables, curd and an apple. Compare the two menus for the large intestine and its bacteria, and say what mealtime habits the cook should add so that either menu supports a healthy digestive system.
questions.a: Menu 1 has no fibre-rich or fermented food, so the large intestine gets little help in making the stool easy to pass and the bacteria have little fibre to break down. Menu 2 has fibre-rich whole-wheat roti, vegetables and apple, which help the large intestine function by making stool easier to pass. Menu 2 also has curd, a fermented food that is good for the digestive system. The cook should add the book's habits: meals at proper timings, mindful eating and avoiding overeating. No menu works well if eaten in a rush or in excess.
s: Menu 1 lacks fibre-rich and fermented foods
Menu 2 fibre-rich foods ease stool
Curd as the fermented food and its benefit
Mealtime habits: timings, mindful eating, no overeating
Judgement: menu 2 better, but habits matter for both

questions.q: Person A's large intestine absorbs water and salts normally. Person B's large intestine absorbs very little of either, though his small intestine works normally. Both eat the same meal. Predict and explain the differences in their stool and in what the body keeps, and say what stays the same for the two.
questions.a: A's waste becomes semi-solid stool because water and some salts are taken from the undigested food. B's waste stays watery, because little water is taken from it. B's body keeps less of the water and salts, which pass out with the stool instead. For both, the nutrients were digested and absorbed in the small intestine before this stage, and the stool, whether semi-solid or watery, is stored in the rectum and expelled through the anus by egestion.
s: A: semi-solid stool because water and salts are taken
B: watery waste because little water is absorbed
B's body keeps less water and salts
Nutrient absorption in the small intestine is the same for both
Both store in the rectum and egest through the anus

questions.q: Hema lives for weeks on food that has almost no fibre. Which of the following would NOT be expected?
questions.a: Her small intestine stops absorbing nutrients
o: Her small intestine stops absorbing nutrients
Her stool becomes harder and more difficult to pass
Her large intestine finds it harder to function properly
Her bacteria get less fibre to break down in the large intestine

questions.q: Four people describe their eating routine. Whose routine follows all the advice for digestive health that your book gives from Ayurveda and modern nutrition?
questions.a: Hema eats at fixed times, eats attentively and stops before she overeats
o: Hema eats at fixed times, eats attentively and stops before she overeats
Irfan eats at fixed times and attentively, but always takes a third helping
Jaya eats a moderate amount, but at different hours and while watching a screen
Karan eats a moderate amount at fixed times, but swallows each bite in seconds while reading messages

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about the large intestine.
Statement 1: Its bacteria break down undigested food, especially fibre, and produce essential nutrients.
Statement 2: Fermented foods like curd and kanji harm the digestive system because they contain bacteria.
Statement 3: Fibre-rich foods help it function properly by making the stool easier to pass.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only
o: 1 and 3 only
1 and 2 only
2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q: Meera says: 'Fibre that stays undigested is not wasted. It reaches the large intestine, where bacteria break it down, and the fibre also helps the stool pass easily.' Do you agree? Support your answer from the book.
questions.a: Yes. The book says the large intestine contains bacteria that break down undigested food, especially fibre, and produce essential nutrients. It also says fibre-rich food helps the large intestine function properly by making the stool easier to pass. So undigested fibre does useful work on both counts.
s: Verdict: agrees
Bacteria break down undigested food, especially fibre
Fibre makes the stool easier to pass

questions.q:
At a school 'Food Across India' fair, the science club can stock exactly two items for a gut-friendly corner, one for each child, with Rs 24 per child. The stalls offer: kanji Rs 8, fruit salad Rs 15, fried chips Rs 10, sweet jalebi Rs 12, curd Rs 6 and gundruk soup Rs 14. 120 children will visit.
(a) Which of the six items are fermented foods, according to your book?
(b) What does the fruit salad give the large intestine and how does it help?
(c) Which pairs of one fruit salad and one fermented item fit Rs 24 per child, and what does each cost for 120 children?
(d) Choose the cheapest pair that gives two different benefits and justify the choice.
questions.a: (a) Kanji, curd and gundruk. (b) Fibre, which helps the large intestine function properly by making the stool easier to pass. (c) Fruit salad + kanji = Rs 23, which is Rs 2,760 for 120 children; fruit salad + curd = Rs 21, which is Rs 2,520. Fruit salad + gundruk = Rs 29 does not fit. (d) Fruit salad + curd, at Rs 2,520: it gives fibre to ease the stool and a fermented food that is good for the digestive system; chips and jalebi give neither.
s: Part (a): kanji, curd, gundruk
Part (b): fibre eases stool
Part (c): 23 and 21 per child; 2,760 and 2,520; gundruk pair 29 does not fit
Part (d): fruit salad and curd with the two benefits

questions.q:
Suppose 300 mL of watery undigested material enters the large intestine in a day and 100 mL of stool leaves the body. Assume the difference is all water.
(a) How much water did the large intestine take from the waste?
(b) What else does it take, and what does the removal do to the nature of the waste?
questions.a: (a) 300 - 100 = 200 mL. (b) It also takes some salts; the waste becomes semi-solid, which is called stool.
s: Part (a): 200 mL
Part (b): some salts, waste becomes semi-solid stool

questions.q:
A grandmother says a very big dinner eaten late while scrolling through a phone is 'good for digestion because of the ginger and cumin in it'.
(a) What does the Charaka Samhita note say about spices like ginger, black pepper and cumin?
(b) Which two other practices from the book does her dinner break?
questions.a: (a) Their judicious use enhances digestion; it does not say a heavy meal becomes healthy by adding them. (b) It breaks mindful eating (scrolling while eating) and avoiding overeating (a very big dinner).
s: Part (a): judicious use of spices enhances digestion
Part (b): mindful eating and avoiding overeating

questions.q: An investigation shows that in a healthy man the waste collects in the lowest part of his large intestine for some hours after it is formed, and leaves the body only later. How should this be read?
questions.a: Normal: stool waits in the rectum until the body is ready
o: Normal: stool waits in the rectum until the body is ready
Abnormal: stool should leave the body at the moment it is formed
Normal: nutrients are absorbed there during the waiting time
Abnormal: stool should wait in the stomach, not in the large intestine

questions.q: A farmer keeps 5 cows. Going by the time your book gives for a cow's daily chewing of its food, the herd spends ___ cow-hours a day chewing.
Write two clues, using only what your book says, from which a classmate can say an animal is a ruminant. Then say which clue is the deciding one.
questions.a: Clues: it is a grass-eating animal that partly chews and swallows the grass into its stomach; the partly digested food is brought back to its mouth and chewed gradually. The deciding clue is the return of the partly digested food to the mouth for chewing.
s: Two clues consistent with the book
Names the return of food to the mouth as the deciding clue

questions.q: A veterinarian finds that a goat's partly digested food is no longer coming back from its stomach to its mouth, although the goat eats well. Which step of its digestion is most affected?
questions.a: Thorough chewing of the partly digested food in the mouth
o: Thorough chewing of the partly digested food in the mouth
The wave-like pushing of food down the food pipe
The grinding of food by a gizzard with the help of grit
The passing of digested nutrients into the blood

questions.q:
Ramesh keeps 20 cows. They graze 10 hours a day. To save fodder he considers Plan A: graze 17 hours a day. Plan B: graze 15 hours a day and buy extra fodder at Rs 40 per cow per day. His vet says the cows' daily chewing time of the food must not be cut. Assume grazing and chewing do not overlap and each day has 24 hours.
(a) What do the cows do during their chewing hours, and where does that food come from?
(b) How many hours remain for chewing under Plan A and under Plan B, if a cow needs the time your book gives?
(c) What does this chewing do for digestion, and what would be lost if it were cut?
(d) Choose a plan and justify it, including the daily cost.
questions.a: (a) They bring partly digested food back from the stomach to the mouth and chew it gradually (rumination). (b) Plan A leaves 24 - 17 = 7 hours, less than 8; Plan B leaves 24 - 15 = 9 hours, which is enough. (c) The thoroughly chewed food passes down the alimentary canal for further digestion; if the chewing is cut, less of the food is chewed thoroughly before further digestion. (d) Plan B, since Plan A cuts the 8 hours of chewing; it costs 20 x Rs 40 = Rs 800 a day for the extra fodder.
s: Part (a): rumination of food brought back from the stomach
Part (b): 7 hours versus 9 hours against 8
Part (c): thorough chewing before further digestion
Part (d): Plan B at Rs 800 a day, with reason

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about digestion in some animals.
Statement 1: A hen's gizzard sends partly digested food back to its mouth for chewing.
Statement 2: In a ruminant, partly digested food is brought back from the stomach to the mouth and chewed gradually.
Statement 3: Birds swallow grit because it is digested to give them energy.
Which of the statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 only
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
A poultry farmer keeps one batch of hens on whole grain with no stones or grit in their run.
(a) Predict what will happen to the breaking up of the grain in their gizzards, compared with hens that find grit.
(b) Explain your prediction with the working of the gizzard.
questions.a: (a) The grain will be broken up less well. (b) A bird's food is broken down by the contraction and relaxation of the gizzard's walls, often with the help of grit; without grit the walls have less help in breaking the hard grain.
s: Part (a): grain broken less well
Part (b): gizzard walls work often with grit

questions.q: Ravi says: 'A cow resting and chewing is still digesting. It is just like a person chewing a roti before swallowing it.' Do you agree? Explain.
questions.a: Partly right. The cow's chewing is part of digestion, since it is rumination and the thoroughly chewed food goes on for further digestion. But it is not just like a person's chewing: the cow chews partly digested food that has been brought back from its stomach to its mouth, whereas a person chews the food once, before it has been in the stomach.
s: Verdict: partly right
Right: rumination is part of digestion
Wrong: the cow chews food returned from the stomach, a person chews before swallowing

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A cow keeps chewing even when it is not grazing.
Reason (R): A cow brings partly digested food back from its stomach to its mouth for gradual chewing.
questions.a: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q: A student writes: 'All animals digest like humans: the teeth crush the food and then it moves down the canal.' Test this statement for a human, a cow and a hen. Say what is right in each case, what is not, and what the book concludes about animals.
questions.a: Human: teeth crush and chew the food, and the food is moved on, so it fits. Cow: it does swallow food and it goes on for further digestion, but the cow first partly chews and swallows the grass, partly digests it in the stomach and brings it back to the mouth to chew gradually. Hen: it has no teeth, so crushing is done by the gizzard whose walls contract and relax, often with grit. So the statement is only true for the human. The book concludes that animals show variations in the structure and function of the alimentary canal, adapted to different kinds of food.
s: Human: statement fits
Cow: first partial chewing, stomach, return and gradual chewing
Hen: no teeth, gizzard with grit
Verdict: true only for the human
Book's conclusion: variation adapted to kinds of food

questions.q: Four animals are observed. W keeps moving its jaws while resting though it is not eating. X swallows small stones along with its food. Y chews its food once in its mouth with teeth and swallows it. Z swallows the animals it preys upon. Which row labels them correctly?
questions.a: W: buffalo, X: hen, Y: human, Z: python
o: W: buffalo, X: hen, Y: human, Z: python
W: hen, X: buffalo, Y: python, Z: human
W: human, X: python, Y: hen, Z: buffalo
W: python, X: human, Y: buffalo, Z: hen

questions.q:
A poultry farm has three batches, each of 250 hens eating 100 kg of grain a day. Batch A gets grit, batch B gets no grit, and batch C gets no grit but pre-crushed grain. Whole grain pieces left unbroken: A 6%, B 30%, C 2%. Assume unbroken grain is wasted and costs Rs 25 per kg. For a 30-day month, grit costs Rs 1,200 and crushing the grain costs Rs 3,000.
(a) Which chamber breaks the grain in a hen, and how does it work?
(b) How many kg of grain are wasted in a month in A and in B?
(c) Explain from the book why B wastes more than A.
(d) Compare the total monthly cost (waste plus extra cost) of A and C and decide which batch's method the farm should use.
questions.a: (a) The gizzard; its walls contract and relax to break the food, often with the help of grit. (b) A: 100 x 0.06 x 30 = 180 kg. B: 100 x 0.30 x 30 = 900 kg. (c) B has no grit, so the gizzard walls have less help in breaking the hard grain, and more is left whole. (d) A: 180 x 25 + 1,200 = Rs 5,700. C: 60 x 25 + 3,000 = Rs 4,500. The farm should use C's method, which is Rs 1,200 cheaper a month.
s: Part (a): gizzard, wall contraction and relaxation with grit
Part (b): 180 kg and 900 kg
Part (c): no grit means less help to the gizzard
Part (d): Rs 5,700 versus Rs 4,500, choose C's method

questions.q: A bird-watcher notes that sparrows swallow many small stones after eating hard dry seeds but only a few after eating soft berries. Which explanation fits the book best?
questions.a: Hard seeds need more breaking, which grit helps the gizzard do
o: Hard seeds need more breaking, which grit helps the gizzard do
The stones are digested into nutrients that hard seeds lack
The stones bring partly digested seeds back to the mouth to be chewed
Sparrows chew seeds with teeth that the stones keep sharp

questions.q: A friend says: 'A hen ruminates after pecking grain, because its gizzard keeps moving.' Show that the hen's gizzard movement is not rumination.
questions.a: Rumination means bringing partly digested food back from the stomach to the mouth and chewing it gradually. A hen has no teeth and no such returning of food. Its gizzard breaks the food by contraction and relaxation of its walls, often with the help of grit, and the food then goes on down the canal.
s: Defines rumination as food returned to the mouth
The hen has no teeth and nothing returns to the mouth
Gizzard works by wall contraction and relaxation, often with grit

questions.q: A farmer asks why his cow keeps its jaws moving in the shed with no fodder in the trough, and whether he should worry. Write a three-point explanation covering where the food in her mouth came from, why it takes so long, and what would be affected if she stopped.
questions.a: The food in her mouth is partly digested food brought back from her stomach, so she is not eating anything fresh. She chews it gradually and thoroughly, which takes about 8 hours a day. If she stopped, the food would not be thoroughly chewed before passing down the alimentary canal for further digestion, so the farmer should see a vet.
s: Source: partly digested food returned from the stomach
Gradual chewing for about 8 hours a day
If stopped, thorough chewing before further digestion is lost

questions.q:
(a) Which of buffalo, goat, hen and human are ruminants, according to your book?
(b) What single observation separates a ruminant from a hen when both are at rest after a meal?
questions.a: (a) The buffalo and the goat. (b) A ruminant keeps chewing food that has been brought back to its mouth from its stomach, while a hen brings nothing back to its mouth and has no teeth.
s: Part (a): buffalo and goat
Part (b): the return of partly digested food to the mouth

questions.q:
Divya says: 'The food a cow brings back to its mouth to chew is just the fresh grass it ate earlier, unchanged.'
(a) Is she right?
(b) What has happened to the food in the meantime, and where does it go after thorough chewing?
questions.a: (a) No. (b) It has been partly digested in the stomach; after being chewed thoroughly it passes down the alimentary canal for further digestion.
s: Part (a): no, the food is partly digested
Part (b): partial digestion in the stomach, then down the canal for further digestion

questions.q: Compare digestion in a cow and in a bird on four points: how the food is broken up, where this happens, what helps and what the animal swallows. Then say which of the two does more of its chewing in the mouth and why.
questions.a: Cow: the grass is partly chewed and swallowed; it is partly digested in the stomach, then brought back to the mouth, where it is chewed gradually for about 8 hours a day. Bird: it has no teeth, so food is broken in the gizzard by the contraction and relaxation of its walls; the bird swallows grit (small stones), which helps. The cow does more of its chewing in the mouth, because a bird has no teeth and breaks its food in the gizzard instead.
s: Cow: partly chewed, swallowed, partly digested, returned
Bird: gizzard, wall contraction and relaxation
Grit swallowed to help
Conclusion: the cow chews in the mouth, the bird does not

questions.q:
Suppose a person spends 20 minutes a day chewing food, while a cow spends the number of hours your book gives.
(a) How many times as long as the person's chewing time is the cow's?
(b) Name the feature of a cow's digestion that explains most of the difference.
questions.a: (a) 8 hours = 480 minutes, and 480 / 20 = 24 times. (b) Rumination: the cow brings partly digested food back from the stomach to the mouth and chews it again gradually.
s: Part (a): 480 / 20 = 24 times
Part (b): rumination, chewing the returned food again

questions.q: Which observation would make you doubt that an animal is a ruminant?
questions.a: It never brings swallowed food back to its mouth
o: It never brings swallowed food back to its mouth
It keeps chewing for hours without eating any fresh grass
It swallows grass after chewing it only a little
It is a grass-eating animal on a farm

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Birds can break down hard grains even though they have no teeth.
Reason (R): Birds do this by bringing partly digested grains back from the stomach to the mouth for gradual chewing.
questions.a: A is true but R is false.
o: A and R are both true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.

questions.q:
The 12 guards of a housing society smoke at its gate, and the wind often carries the smoke to the balcony of Imran's flat, where his grandfather and his baby sister sit every evening. The society must choose between two plans. The corner plan: a smoking corner behind the community hall, beside the park where 20 children play every evening and downwind of Imran's block. The ban plan: a complete ban inside the compound, so the guards would smoke outside the gate, where 15 schoolchildren wait for their bus.
(a) What does the book say smoking releases into the air, and what is the harm to those who breathe it called?
(b) Which of the groups the book names as specially at risk are present in Imran's family?
(c) Count the people from the specially at-risk groups that each plan exposes, taking the park children, the bus-stop children and Imran's family members from (b).
(d) Recommend a plan and justify it, saying what risk remains.
questions.a: (a) Toxic chemicals; the harm to non-smokers who breathe the polluted air is passive smoking. (b) A child (his baby sister) and an elderly person (his grandfather). (c) Corner plan: 20 children + 2 family members = 22. Ban plan: 15 children. (d) The ban plan, exposes fewer people from the at-risk groups (15 against 22) and removes the smoke from the compound; the remaining risk is to the 15 children at the bus stop, so the society should also ask the guards not to smoke near the stop.
s: Part (a): toxic chemicals, passive smoking
Part (b): a child and an elderly person
Part (c): 22 for the corner plan, 15 for the ban plan
Part (d): ban, with the remaining risk named

questions.q: A student describes the journey of one breath. Which description is fully correct?
questions.a: Nostrils, nasal passages, windpipe with two branches, finer branches, alveoli
o: Nostrils, nasal passages, windpipe with two branches, finer branches, alveoli
Nostrils, windpipe, nasal passages, two branches into the lungs, finer branches, alveoli
Nostrils, nasal passages, alveoli, finer branches in each lung, then the windpipe
Nostrils, nasal passages, windpipe with one branch for each nostril, then alveoli

questions.q: Tight bandages stop a boy's ribs from moving up and outwards, but his diaphragm moves down normally when he breathes in. What is the most likely result?
questions.a: Air still enters, but the chest grows less than usual, so he takes in less air
o: Air still enters, but the chest grows less than usual, so he takes in less air
No air can enter at all, because breathing in needs ribs and diaphragm to move together
More air than usual enters, because the diaphragm now does all the work alone
Air is pushed out of the lungs, because the ribs are held in tightly by the bandage

questions.q: A student draws a flow chart for one breath: Nostrils - windpipe - nasal passages - lungs - alveoli. (a) Find the error. (b) Write the correct order, including what the windpipe does before the lungs. (c) Name the part where oxygen finally reaches the blood.
questions.a: (a) The windpipe and the nasal passages are swapped; air goes through the nasal passages before the windpipe. (b) Nostrils, nasal passages, windpipe, which forms two branches that enter the two lungs, finer branches in the lungs, alveoli. (c) The alveoli.
s: Error: windpipe and nasal passages swapped
Correct order with two branches into the lungs
Alveoli

questions.q: Tara concludes from Activity 9.3: 'Exhaled air has carbon dioxide, so inhaled air must have none.' Is her conclusion right? Explain.
questions.a: No. In the activity the lime water in the tube with ordinary air stayed clear and that in the tube with exhaled air turned milky, which shows exhaled air has more carbon dioxide than inhaled air. The test shows 'more', not that inhaled air has no carbon dioxide at all, so her conclusion does not follow.
s: Verdict: no
Evidence from the two tubes
The test shows more, not none

questions.q: Before a race, a coach teaches deep breathing. Using the mechanism of breathing, explain how a deeper breath in and a complete breath out are achieved. Include the ribs, the diaphragm, the space inside the chest and the lungs, and say how the model of Activity 9.2 would show a deeper breath.
questions.a: For a deeper breath in, the ribs move further up and outwards and the diaphragm moves further down. This increases the space inside the chest more than usual, so more air enters the lungs. For a complete breath out, the ribs move down and inwards and the diaphragm moves up, which reduces the space and pushes more air out of the lungs. In the model, pulling the rubber sheet further down would inflate the balloons (lungs) more, and releasing it upwards would deflate them.
s: Deeper inhalation: ribs further up and out, diaphragm further down
Chest space increases more, more air enters
Exhalation: ribs down and in, diaphragm up
Space reduces, air pushed out of the lungs
Model: sheet pulled further down inflates balloons more

questions.q: In the model of Activity 9.2 a student replaces the rubber sheet with a stiff wooden board fixed tightly to the base of the bottle. When she tries to pull it down, what does this show about breathing?
questions.a: The balloons cannot inflate, so the diaphragm must move down for air to enter the lungs
o: The balloons cannot inflate, so the diaphragm must move down for air to enter the lungs
The balloons inflate even more, which shows that the diaphragm is not needed
The balloons deflate, which shows that the ribs push air out of the lungs
The bottle fills with air directly, which shows air enters the chest without lungs

questions.q:
In Activity 9.3 the two test tubes get equal amounts of freshly prepared lime water.
(a) What is kept the same in the two tubes, and what is the one thing changed?
(b) Why does this make the milky colour in one tube a fair sign of something in the air?
questions.a: (a) The amount and freshness of the lime water are kept the same; the air passed into the lime water is changed (ordinary air with a pichkari in tube A, exhaled air blown with a straw in tube B). (b) Since only the air differs, the milky colour of tube B can be put down to the exhaled air, which contains more carbon dioxide.
s: Part (a): same lime water, different air
Part (b): only the air differs, so milkiness is due to carbon dioxide in exhaled air

questions.q: Evaluate the model of Activity 9.2 as a model of breathing. Say what the balloons and the rubber sheet stand for, what the model shows correctly, and two things about the real breathing system that the model leaves out or simplifies. Then give a verdict on how far the model can be trusted.
questions.a: The balloons stand for the lungs and the rubber sheet for the diaphragm. The model shows correctly that pulling the diaphragm down increases the space and air inflates the lungs, while releasing it upwards deflates them. It leaves out the ribs, which move up and outwards in inhalation, and it shows two simple balloons instead of the windpipe's branches dividing into finer branches that end in alveoli. Verdict: it models the diaphragm's role well but not the whole mechanism, so it should be used alongside the description of the ribs and the branching lungs.
s: Balloons are lungs, sheet is diaphragm
What the model shows correctly: down inflates, up deflates
Leaves out the movement of the ribs
Leaves out the branching to alveoli
Verdict on how far to trust it

questions.q:
Two designs are proposed for Activity 9.3. Meera's design uses two tubes A and B with equal fresh lime water: ordinary air is passed into A with a pichkari and breath is blown into B with a straw. Salim's design uses one tube: he blows his breath into the lime water and watches whether it turns milky. The class has 40 children and 6 test tubes, and each group needs its own set-up; the 40 children are split as equally as possible.
(a) What would a milky tube B show?
(b) Why can Salim's single tube not support the statement that exhaled air has more carbon dioxide than inhaled air?
(c) How many set-ups can the class make with each design, and how many children does the largest group have?
(d) Choose a design and justify it, naming what it costs.
questions.a: (a) That exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than the air we inhale, since lime water turns milky with carbon dioxide. (b) There is no tube with inhaled air to compare with, so it only shows the breath has some carbon dioxide. (c) Meera: 6 / 2 = 3 set-ups, the largest group is 14 children (40 / 3 = 13.3). Salim: 6 set-ups, the largest group is 7 children (40 / 6 = 6.7). (d) Meera's design, because the aim is a comparison of exhaled and inhaled air; the cost is bigger groups of 14 instead of 7.
s: Part (a): exhaled air has more carbon dioxide
Part (b): no inhaled-air tube to compare
Part (c): 3 set-ups, 14 children; 6 set-ups, 7 children
Part (d): Meera's design, cost is bigger groups

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The rib cage protects the lungs.
Reason (R): On inhalation the ribs move up and outwards.
questions.a: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
o: A and R are both true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:

(a) Arrange breathing, water and food in the order of how long we can do without each, shortest first.
(b) Give one reason, from what breathing brings in, why the shortest one is so urgent.

s: Part (a): breathing, water, food
Part (b): oxygen is needed to release energy

questions.q: A student writes: 'In one inhalation the ribs move up and outwards while the diaphragm moves up.' Show that this cannot describe a real breath in.

questions.q:

questions.q: Rohit says: 'After a hard run, more respiration is going on in my leg muscles, so the equation of respiration tells me my exhaled air should now carry more carbon dioxide than it did at rest.' Do you agree? Support your answer from the book.
questions.a: Yes. Respiration breaks down glucose with oxygen to give carbon dioxide, water and energy, and it takes place inside the body. When the muscles do more respiration, more carbon dioxide is formed, the blood carries it to the alveoli, and so the exhaled air carries more of it than at rest.
s: Verdict: agrees
Equation: respiration forms carbon dioxide
Blood carries the extra carbon dioxide to the alveoli

questions.q:
Priya's club measures two air samples. Sample P has 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide. Sample Q has 16% oxygen and 5% carbon dioxide. Priya says: 'Only 5 of the 21 parts of oxygen are used, so the air in a sealed hall can be breathed again and again.'
(a) Which sample is exhaled air? Give a reason from the equation of respiration.
(b) What percentage of the oxygen in P was used (to one decimal place), and how many times higher is the carbon dioxide in Q than in P?
(c) Through which part of the lungs does the extra carbon dioxide enter the air, and what brings it there?
(d) The school plans a two-hour yoga class in a sealed hall. Using your figures, advise for or against and give your reason.
questions.a: (a) Q, because respiration uses oxygen and forms carbon dioxide, so exhaled air has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide. (b) 5/21 = 23.8% of the oxygen; carbon dioxide 5/0.04 = 125 times higher. (c) The alveoli; the blood brings the carbon dioxide from the body to them. (d) Against. Each breath uses nearly a quarter of the oxygen and raises the carbon dioxide 125 times, and in a sealed hall the same air would be breathed again, so the oxygen would keep falling and the carbon dioxide rising (an inference from the figures); the hall should be ventilated.
s: Part (a): Q, with the equation as reason
Part (b): 23.8% and 125 times
Part (c): alveoli, brought by the blood
Part (d): advise against, reasoning from the figures

questions.q: The glucose from a runner's digested food and the oxygen from her alveoli must both reach her leg muscles. Which statement correctly describes how they get there?

Glucose goes by the food pipe and oxygen by the blood vessels
Oxygen is carried by the heart alone, while glucose is carried by the blood

questions.a: (a) Glucose, the simple sugar obtained from the digested food. (b) Oxygen helps to break down glucose and release the energy.

questions.q: A friend says: 'The more I breathe, the more energy I get.' Evaluate this statement using what breathing brings in, what respiration needs, and what happens to the breathing rate when the muscles work harder. Give a verdict.
questions.a: Breathing brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. Respiration needs both glucose, which comes from digested food, and oxygen, so extra air without glucose cannot release extra energy. But when the muscles work harder and need more energy, the breathing rate rises to supply the oxygen they need for respiration. So breathing does support energy release, but it does not create energy by itself. Verdict: partly right.
s: Breathing brings in oxygen
Respiration needs glucose as well as oxygen
More air without glucose gives no extra energy
Harder work raises the breathing rate to supply oxygen
Verdict: partly right

questions.q: Using the word equation of respiration, show that exhaled air must contain less oxygen and more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.
questions.a: Respiration uses oxygen and produces carbon dioxide. So oxygen is removed and carbon dioxide added in the body. Therefore exhaled air has less oxygen (16-17% compared with 21%) and more carbon dioxide (4-5% compared with 0.04%).
s: Oxygen is used in respiration
Carbon dioxide is produced
Compares percentages

questions.q:
A student says: 'If the heart stopped but the lungs kept working, oxygen would still reach every part of the body.'
(a) Give your verdict.
(b) Explain it using what the heart does.
questions.a: (a) False; the claim is wrong. (b) The heart pumps blood through the blood vessels, and the blood carries the oxygen, nutrients and other substances to all parts of the body; if the pumping stopped, the oxygen taken in at the alveoli would not be carried to the body.
s: Part (a): verdict that the claim is wrong
Part (b): the heart pumps blood that carries the oxygen

questions.q: A chart gives three air samples. Sample 1: oxygen 21%, carbon dioxide 0.04%. Sample 2: oxygen 17%, carbon dioxide 4%. Sample 3: oxygen 12%, carbon dioxide 9%, from an unknown source. Which sample is the exhaled air of a healthy person?

Sample 3, because respiration uses up almost all the oxygen of inhaled air

questions.q: A spoonful of rice is eaten at breakfast. Trace how its starch is turned into energy in a leg muscle during a 100 m race. Include the mouth, the small intestine, the circulatory system, the lungs and the word equation of respiration, and say where the waste of this energy release goes.
questions.a: In the mouth, saliva begins breaking the starch into sugar. In the small intestine the digested food passes by absorption into the blood in its walls. The circulatory system, with the heart pumping blood through blood vessels, carries the glucose to the leg muscle. Oxygen comes in by breathing, passes from the alveoli into the blood and is carried to the muscle. There respiration takes place: Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. The blood carries the carbon dioxide back to the alveoli, from where it is breathed out.
s: Mouth and small intestine: starch to sugar, absorption into blood
Circulatory system carries glucose to the muscle
Oxygen from the alveoli carried by the blood
Word equation of respiration in the muscle
Carbon dioxide carried back to the alveoli and exhaled

questions.a: (i) Oxygen will find it harder to pass from the alveoli into the blood. (ii) Carbon dioxide will find it harder to pass from the blood into the alveoli to be breathed out. Carbon dioxide release reduced
Less oxygen means less energy released

questions.q:

(b) Would its exhaled air hold more or less carbon dioxide than ours, and why?
questions.a: (a) Half of 21 is 10.5, so about 10.5% oxygen would be left in the exhaled air. (b) More carbon dioxide, because the more oxygen is used in respiration, the more carbon dioxide is formed.
s: Part (b): more carbon dioxide because more respiration

questions.q:
Kabir breathes 18 times a minute at rest and 40 times a minute right after his 100 m race. Assume each breath takes in 500 mL of air and gives out 500 mL, and that his exhaled air holds 16.5% oxygen both at rest and after the race.
(a) How much oxygen does his body keep from one breath?
(b) How much oxygen does it keep in a minute at rest and in a minute right after the race, and how many times as much is the second?
(c) Which process needs the extra oxygen, and which system carries it to his leg muscles?
(d) Predict whether his exhaled air right after the race holds more or less carbon dioxide than the book's 4 to 5%, giving a reason from the equation.
questions.a: (a) Inhaled air has 21% oxygen, so 500 mL holds 105 mL; exhaled air holds 82.5 mL; he keeps 22.5 mL. (b) At rest 18 x 22.5 = 405 mL a minute; after the race 40 x 22.5 = 900 mL a minute; 900/405 = about 2.2 times. (c) Respiration in the muscles, which releases the energy for the run; the circulatory system carries the oxygen. (d) More than 4 to 5%, since the muscles do more respiration, forming more carbon dioxide, which the blood carries to the alveoli; this is a prediction from the equation, because the book gives the 4 to 5% only as a general figure.
s: Part (a): 22.5 mL
Part (b): 405 mL, 900 mL, about 2.2 times
Part (c): respiration; the circulatory system
Part (d): more carbon dioxide, with the equation as reason

questions.q:
A village pond is drying up in summer. Volunteers find 30 tadpoles, 20 fish and 12 adult frogs in it. They have a bucket that carries 25 animals a trip, and the mud will stay wet enough for only 2 trips.

Part (b): lungs on land, skin in water

Part (d): carry fish and tadpoles only, frogs breathe on land

Most aquatic animals have gills, fish are an example

Frog: lungs on land
Frog: skin in water

Link between organ and habitat

questions.a: Goldfish: water, because gills exchange gases between blood and the gases dissolved in water. Adult frogs: both land and water, because they use lungs on land and skin in water.
